newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Long bond signals worries for HK grade A offices.
newsitem.headline: Long bond signals worries for HK grade A offices.

text.p: Yields on Hong Kong grade A commercial property have been tracking the yield on the U.S. long bond, which could be cause for concern since the bond yield appears to have peaked, analysts say.

Property yields are the returns landlords get from rentals compared to costs. While they are not directly tied to U.S. bond yields, the peg between the U.S. and Hong Kong dollars has caused local assets to move in line with U.S. assets.
"Basically, they are acting like a long bond," Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at HG Asia Securities, said of property yields based on spot office prices to spot rents.

The correlation is especially handy because the grade A office market is not very liquid and identifying benchmark deals useful for calculating property yields can be difficult, so the long bond yield acts as a good proxy.
And knowing the property yield is vital for stock investors since it can help determine the profitability, share price and dividend payout of property investment companies.
"The dividend yield (of property investment companies) moves in line with the U.S. long bond yield," said Raymond Ngai, senior investment analyst at UBS Securities (East Asia).
The recent trend in the U.S. long bond has most strategists sitting on the edge of their portfolios.

The bond yield bottomed out near 6.3 percent at the end of November and then surged to 6.9 percent in late January. But many analysts do not expect it to move much higher, and it has eased back to around 6.6 percent.
"I expect the long-bond yield to stay restrained, below 7.0 percent. It may rise up temporarily but the long-term trend is still down," said van der Kamp.
If bond yields bottomed out in late November, then the yield on Hong Kong office property should have troughed around the end of November and capital values reached a cycle peak.

That was the view of some analysts in late November when Hysan Development Ltd bought a major investment property at an average price of HK$17,000 per sq ft, which indicated a pre-tax yield of less than five percent.
"Based on that sales price, I'm using a yield of 4.5 percent to evaluate Hysan's entire (property) portfolio," said Ngai.
Ngai said that yield was lower than the 5.5 percent that he had previously used and which he believed was a long-term strategic benchmark of the company.
Yields on grade A commercial property have averaged 5.8 percent in the past five years, with the highest rates seen in 1992 at 7.0 percent.
The latest government statistics show that yields were trending at 5.0 percent as at end-September 1996.
The short-term rise in the long bond yield from 6.3 percent to 6.9 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 might imply that property yields have gone up and that capital values are poised to slump.
But the November sale price of the Entertainment Building, however, suggests yields continued to fall.
Property consultants said the average HK$17,000 per sq ft sales price and estimated rental rate of HK$50 to HK$52 per sq ft gave a gross yield of about 3.6 percent.
And with bond yields seen capped longer term, this may indicate little upside for property yields, analysts said.

"There are four considerations in determining yield on commercial property -- long-term interest rates, expected growth in rental income, the risk associated with it and the propensity to own," said UBS's Ngai.

Using the 30-year U.S. bond yield as a competitive asset to gauge the trend of office yields and considering forecasts for the other three indicators, office yields are forecast to hover about the five percent level, he said.

The fundamental view on the Hong Kong property market sees property investment yields moving up in line with the upturn in the Hong Kong economy, spurring greater demand for office space and helping perk up sluggish rental rates.

"Rental rates on grade A commercial property rose between two to three percent in 1996 and most of that in the last quarter," said Adrian Ngan, director of Peregrine Securities. "I am forecasting about a 15 percent rise in rentals in 1997."
Ngan said the rise in rental rates in late 1996 was just a warming up, the early part of the expansion phase of the cycle.
Bears are much more cautious.
Ngai forecast a fall in rental rates of 2.7 percent in 1997 before a turnaround in 1998 with a rise of 7.1 percent.
